source.title: Language models transmit behavioural traits through hidden signals in data
source.authors: Alex Cloud; Minh Le; James Chua; Jan Betley; A. Sztyber-Betley; Sören Mindermann; Jacob Hilton; Samuel Marks; Owain Evans

page_placements.theme: Toy and classifier analogues: shared initialisation

record.tranche_reason: The paper directly applies teacher-generated, filtered-data fine-tuning and measures student trait behaviour, including comparisons across base models and an in-context-only condition.
record.gate_note: Rows record the paper's own trait-transfer outcomes, controls, cross-model comparisons, prompt-only comparison, sequence-shuffling result and theoretical result. MMLU changes are not rows because they measure general capability, not a claimed trait. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: This is the peer-reviewed Nature version of the original subliminal-learning paper (same authors, same experiments as arXiv:2507.14805). It tests A–D and F directly, and E only partly. It is an original source, so no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Teacher outputs carry hidden trait information, and a sufficiently similar student (shared or behaviourally matched initialization) acquires the traits through fine-tuning despite filtering. The authors flag this as a safety risk for distillation.
record.recipe_differences: The article reports the teacher-output generation, filtering and student fine-tuning procedure described by the original Subliminal Learning source; no distinct recipe difference is stated.
record.method_sensitivity: Transmission depends on teacher-student model match: mismatched model types generally do not transfer, with GPT-4.1/GPT-4o as an exception. Open-weight animal effects vary by target animal and are more consistent for Qwen2.5-7B when evaluation prompts include number prefixes. Story and multiple-choice evaluations show weaker effects than favourite-preference prompts. Shuffling number order strongly reduces transmission. The evaluation suffix is reported to increase effect sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST MLP student distilled on auxiliary logits of noise inputs recovers digit accuracy only with shared or behaviourally cloned initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal learning in toy classifiers requires shared or behaviourally matched initialization, largely independent of architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-4.1 nano prompted as a classifier detects latent animal content in the number data at chance level (Extended Data Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Trait signal in the filtered data is not detectable by a prompted model.

record.problems: The authors note that code and CoT prompts are simplistic compared with frontier applications and that what traits can transmit remains open. Some open-weight animal effects are inconsistent. Several result sizes are described qualitatively in the supplied text, while numerical detail is only in figures. The CoT alignment filter has a reported false-positive rate of 37% at the chosen threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows intentionally left out; the main reported trait-transfer outcomes and relevant controls/comparisons are represented.

untested.parts: Full fine-tuning vs LoRA and LoRA-rank sweeps are not tested; only evaluation-format variation is.
Insertion of specific linked tokens into prompts is not tested; only whole-dataset ICL is.
No token-entanglement, divergence-token or steering-direction analysis.

missing.what: Evaluation suffix that mimics training format increases effect sizes

record.verdict_notes: This is the original source (Nature publication of arXiv:2507.14805), so no verdicts are issued. The record uses V1–V6; these are mapped to A–F. The Fig. 5a matrix values are readable in the text and should populate R14–R16.

versions.untested_parts: The main language-model results concern stated animal/tree preferences and misalignment, not every possible trait.
Tests model-family/base-model pairings described in the paper; it does not establish a universal rule for every model or behavioural-matching procedure.
Tests broad misalignment outcomes and false statements, not every alignment-relevant trait.
The paper offers a gradient-based theory and sequence-shuffling evidence, but does not identify a specific signal token or directly probe a steering-vector-like direction.
The paper compares some evaluation formats and prompts, but does not report a student full-fine-tuning comparison or a sweep over student LoRA ranks.
Tests in-context examples of animal-number data with GPT-4.1 nano; it does not test all linked-token prompt constructions or other traits/models.

Fig. 5a cell labels are printed in the text, but the layout is lost.

statements.problem: The statement says nothing specific about this study. Its R23 citation (Qwen2.5-7B effects more consistent with a number-sequence evaluation prefix) fits the evaluation-prompt-format factor.
